extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems covering multiple math domain categories, annotated with fully-specified operation programs corresponding to word problems in the AQuA dataset.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.citeAs: Amini, Aida; Gabriel, Saadia; Lin, Shanchuan; Koncel-Kedziorski, Rik; Choi, Yejin; Hajishirzi, Hannaneh. MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319v1, 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by using problems from the AQuA dataset and carefully annotating those problems with formal operation programs. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies to prune the search space of possible operations. The authors used crowdsourcing to align problems with operation programs through a dynamic annotation platform. Annotators were provided with the problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments, and iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. The platform automatically calculated intermediate results after each submitted operation. Quality control was applied through test questions and annotator accuracy thresholds, and additional validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank an operation program as valid. The authors also expanded annotations to similar AQuA problems by replacing numeric values with generic numbers and using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was the AQuA dataset, specifically solvable English multiple-choice GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems from AQuA.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset significantly enhances the AQuA dataset by fully annotating a portion of solvable problems into formal operation programs. Problems were categorized into domains, noisy and unsolvable AQuA problems were excluded from consideration, and annotations were expanded to closely similar problems by replacing numeric values with generic numbers and matching with Levenshtein distance.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies and a lexicon of domain-specific n-grams. These domains were used to prune the search space of possible operations. The authors carefully studied AQuA and removed from consideration problems that were unsolvable without brute-force, non-narrative problems with no words, and other noisy cases when constructing MathQA from solvable portions of AQuA.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The authors designed a dynamic annotation platform for annotating math word problems with formal operation programs. Annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They sequentially selected an operation from the category-specific list and then selected arguments from valid arguments consisting of numbers in the problem, constants in the problem category, and previous calculations. Annotators could hover over operations to receive hints including arguments, formula, and a short explanation. After each submission, the result was automatically calculated and added as a new valid argument. The platform only accepted programs that included some numbers from the problem and whose final calculation was very close to the correct numeric solution. Validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank the operation program as valid.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The annotation process included quality-control questions, annotator accuracy thresholds, and re-pooling of untrusted annotations if annotator accuracy dropped below a threshold. To evaluate alignment quality, at least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank the operation program as valid for selection. The validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories. Expert evaluation over 500 problems showed that 92% of the annotations were valid, and there was 87% agreement between expert validation and the crowdsourcing validation task.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 annotation program per problem, with validation by 3 validators
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The representation language and dataset aim to improve interpretability of math word problem solvers and provide an extra layer of supervision that can be used to reduce the influence of statistical bias in datasets like AQuA.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses significant unwanted noise and statistical bias in the original AQuA dataset, including incorrect solutions, unsolvable problems, incomplete rationales, duplicates, and cases where models may exploit dataset biases through pattern-matching rather than logical reasoning. The MathQA representation language is presented as a way to reduce the influence of such statistical bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset covers most types of math word problems but omits high-order polynomials and problems where the solutions are entirely nonnumeric. The paper notes that some problems remain unsolvable or have multiple interpretations leading to multiple correct solutions. Sequence problems are beyond the scope of current models and difficult without domain knowledge. The representation language also has limitations, for example lacking some operations such as factorization. The categorization strategy can be noisy because some domain-specific n-grams are ambiguous.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, development, and testing math word problem solvers that map word problems to operation programs. The 37k problems are randomly split into 80/12/8 training/dev/test sets. It is used to train sequence-to-program and category-aware neural models and to evaluate performance on interpretable math word problem solving.
